questions.question: What reagent pair and solvent-related feature define the proposed mechanochemical fertilizer synthesis?

options.A: Eggshell calcite and KH2PO4 react by solvent-free mechanochemical activation
options.B: Eggshell calcite and phosphoric acid react in aqueous solution
options.C: Hydroxyapatite and KOH react in an organic solvent
options.D: Struvite and KH2PO4 react under hydrothermal conditions

questions.rationale: The study uses eggshell waste as a CaCO3 source and solid KH2PO4 without solvent.
questions.evidence_quote: The present article, based on reverse logistic, provides an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) aimed for soil conditioning, by a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste and KH2PO4.

questions.question: What milling conditions first produced identifiable potassium-calcium phosphate phases by XRD?

options.A: At least 2 h and 400 rpm, chiefly K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4
options.B: 15 min at 100 rpm, producing only CaKPO4
options.C: 1 h at 200 rpm, producing hydroxyapatite as the sole phase
options.D: 24 h at 100 rpm, producing only unreacted precursors

questions.rationale: Below 2 h and 400 rpm the patterns showed only reactants; the stated minimum conditions produced phosphate phases.
questions.evidence_quote: The milling process between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm produce a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 (PDF database n° 22-1218 indicated by black columns, and black dash lines guiding the comparison with the samples) and possibly CaKPO4 (PDF database n° 33-1002 indicated by red columns, and red dash lines guiding the comparison with the samples). Bellow these milling parameters (time and milling speed) only the reactants diffraction patterns are found, i.e., no evidence of chemical reaction is observed.

questions.question: How did extended milling affect the phase chemistry relative to the initial mechanochemical products?

options.A: Longer milling initiated secondary reactions including dehydroxylation; CaKPO4 became more evident after 24 h
options.B: Longer milling restored calcite and removed all phosphate products
options.C: Milling time had no effect once the initial phosphate appeared
options.D: Only a 2-h treatment produced CaKPO4, while longer times prevented it

questions.rationale: The paper connects increased milling time with secondary transformations and reports more visible CaKPO4 at 24 h.
questions.evidence_quote: When milling time increases, secondary reactions begin, for example, mechanochemical dehydroxylation of the new formed phosphates.

questions.question: What transformation was associated with heating the milled phosphate mixture to 420 °C?

options.A: Conversion to KCaPO4 through recrystallization and partial thermal dehydration of K3CaH(PO4)2
options.B: Formation of CaCO3 by carbonation of KCaPO4
options.C: Complete conversion to hydroxyapatite through hydration
options.D: No structural change; only physically adsorbed water was removed

questions.rationale: XRD after 420 °C showed KCaPO4, linked to partial dehydration/dimerization of the hydrogen phosphate phase.
questions.evidence_quote: On the other hand, the thermal treatment at 420°C converted the samples to KCaPO4 (PDF database n° 33-1002), which confirms that the related mass loss is associated to recrystallization by the partial thermal dehydration of the K3CaH(PO4)2 phase that may still be present in the samples.

questions.question: How did phosphorus and potassium release kinetics change after mechanochemical processing in 2 wt% citric acid?

options.A: Both nutrients showed slower release and better fit pseudo-second-order kinetics than the precursor
options.B: Both nutrients released faster and fit only intraparticle diffusion
options.C: Potassium release accelerated while phosphorus became undetectable
options.D: The precursor and milled material had identical rates and model fits

questions.rationale: Milling formed slower-dissolving potassium-calcium phosphates, and P and K curves correlated best with pseudo-second-order models.
questions.evidence_quote: But, phosphorus and potassium presented better correlation with pseudo-second order model, considering 'R 2 ' and the values related to concentration at equilibrium time "qe" and "experimental qe" (Table 1 ). For both nutrients there was a substantial decrease of the kinetic constant from KH2PO4 to milled samples, attesting the delay in nutrient supply after mechanochemical processing and certainly related to the formation of potassium calcium phosphate phases (K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4).

questions.question: What contrasting effect did milling have on calcium availability relative to the eggshell precursor?

options.A: The new phosphate phases made calcium more readily available, unlike slowly dissolving eggshell CaCO3
options.B: Milling suppressed calcium release while accelerating only phosphorus
options.C: Calcium release was identical for eggshell and milled samples
options.D: Calcium became available only after the material was calcined at 710 °C

questions.rationale: Calcium release was opposite to P and K trends: the new phases increased Ca bioavailability compared with the calcite precursor.
questions.evidence_quote: Even not possible to compare kinetic constants for the calcium release, it is important to highlight that in this case was observed an opposite effect: the new phosphates phases from milling made calcium readily available. Thus, considering the kinetic behavior, it was observed that these materials would promote better nutrient management by delaying the bioavailability of phosphorus and potassium (which are highly soluble from KH2PO4) and increasing the calcium bioavailability.

questions.question: How did the 2 h/600 rpm sample's phosphorus release in soil compare numerically with KH2PO4?

options.A: It reached 25 mg/kg at day 3 and 45 mg/kg at day 30, versus KH2PO4 at 107 mg/kg by day 3
options.B: It reached 107 mg/kg by day 3, versus KH2PO4 at 45 mg/kg by day 30
options.C: It released no P by day 30, while KH2PO4 reached 25 mg/kg
options.D: Both materials reached 100 mg/kg within 3 days

questions.rationale: The milled sample released P more gradually and recovered about 15% by day 30 versus about 40% of KH2PO4 P after 3 days.
questions.evidence_quote: The temporal profile for the precursor KH2PO4 indicates a P increase from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg after 3 days of release keeping constant after 30 days, representing 40% of total P from precursor (KH2PO4). Differently, for sample 2 h/600 rpm, the phosphorus release is more progressive (from 0 mg/kg to 25 mg/kg at 3 days and 45 mg/kg at 30 days) corresponding to 15% of total P content recovered from the milled sample.

questions.question: At day 2, how did P radial diffusion for the 2 h/600 rpm sample compare with struvite and KH2PO4?

options.A: It reached 1.99 cm, between struvite's no-release result and KH2PO4's 2.62 cm
options.B: It reached 2.62 cm, exceeding KH2PO4 at 1.99 cm
options.C: It matched struvite at zero and remained below detection
options.D: It exceeded both materials at 3.5 cm

questions.rationale: The day-2 diffusion front for the milled sample was intermediate between the low-release struvite and highly soluble KH2PO4.
questions.evidence_quote: At day 2 it is possible to see that struvite was not able to release any phosphorus, while sample 2h/600rpm the P diffusion reach a value of 1.99 cm a significant value compared to 2.62 cm for KH2PO4, a source of P considered extremely soluble.

questions.question: What soil-phase mechanism did the authors propose for the slower P and Ca release of the milled material?

options.A: Hydroxyapatite formed from 3 to 30 days and served as a long-term Ca/P source under acidic soil conditions
options.B: Calcite re-precipitated and permanently sequestered all potassium
options.C: K3CaH(PO4)2 converted to soluble KH2PO4 within the first three days
options.D: Struvite formed and removed calcium from solution

questions.rationale: XRD identified hydroxyapatite in soil residues; the paper describes its slow-release behavior and solubilization with acidification near pH 5.
questions.evidence_quote: The slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation -(Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) (PDF database n° 9-432 indicated by green columns) -identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions (Fig. 7 ).

questions.question: What was the main caveat when comparing soil-release behavior with the citric-acid assay?

options.A: The soil experiments showed the same qualitative trend but generally slower release than 2 wt% citric acid
options.B: Soil release was always faster, so citric acid could not predict trends
options.C: Soil results showed rapid P and K release but no measurable calcium
options.D: The soil assay used a different product and therefore could not be compared

questions.rationale: The authors explicitly note the same behavior but an overall slower profile in soil, plausibly connected with hydroxyapatite formation.
questions.evidence_quote: The soil essays performed indicate the same behavior, but a general slower release trend when compared to citric acid solution (wt 2%) essays, this can be explained by hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) formation, that still an important source of calcium and phosphorus as a long-term slow release fertilizer.
